narrative: Three sisters-in-law - aged 28, 35 and 41 - and their six young children fled together from the Qalamoun region north of Damascus. Before the war they had been a tight family of six cousins growing up as siblings. When war arrived in summer 2015, the men could no longer go outside for fear of being drawn into the fighting, and the family turned to smugglers; without enough money for all twelve to leave at once, the men went ahead first. The three women stayed together, moving between friends' houses as rockets fell and houses were bombed, terrified for the children. In January they set off, traveling first by bus to Idlib near the Turkish border, where smugglers told them the only way was a nine-hour walk across the mountains to Turkey. On a bitter night they trekked over muddy ground; the youngest woman, seven months pregnant with twins, slipped and fell as she scrambled up the paths. They did not stop until they reached Turkey. At the coast the sea was too rough to cross, so they waited a week, then climbed into a flimsy boat at midnight and set out into the darkness. A rescue vessel patrolling Greek waters picked them up and took them to the island of Samos, then by ship to Athens. At the Serbian border, where fences were being erected along the Balkan route, the pregnant woman's waters broke while the others argued with the guards; her twins were delivered by emergency caesarean in a Serbian hospital. Fifteen days later, once she was well enough to leave, they waited for night and took three taxis to the Hungarian border, where they met a wire fence; as dawn broke the guards let them through. That night a taxi took them to Vienna, and from there a train to southern Germany. They spent weeks moving between shelters near Dresden before being assigned a renovated farmhouse in a village southwest of the city. Their husbands were able to visit from their own shelter in Duesseldorf, the first time the children had seen their fathers in more than a year.
